answer.exemplar: Testing the strict check first and building the summary only for records that pass means the slow step runs once per passing record instead of once per record, so the saving grows with the number of failures. Reordering is safe for the printed answer only when the summary does not alter anything the check reads; if the summary writes a field the check tests, the order changes the result and not just the cost.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates the two effects: order changes cost whenever work can be skipped, and it changes the answer only when the two steps touch the same data, so naming the shared field is what makes the answer complete.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two steps read or write anything in common.
questions.learningObjective: explain when reordering two steps changes cost and when it changes the answer
